372.title: The heart's wish
372.hook: pooran hoe chit kee ichhaa: may my heart's longing be fulfilled, my mind rest at Your feet (Chaupai)
372.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite these lines in Chaupai Sahib morning and evening, and they are often quoted in Sikh teaching as a prayer for the longing to stay near God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chaupai's first line, and your line, keep me by the hand. Did you get to steady someone today? Now the second line, about the heart. Day three hundred seventy-two.

Ask a child what they wish for and you'll get a list. A puppy, a bike, to stay up late. Ask a teenager and the list changes. Ask someone in their forties and it changes again. Ask someone at the end of a long life and the list usually gets very short. Often it's one or two things, and they're almost never things you can buy. Somewhere underneath all the lists, there's a deepest wish. Most of us rarely say it out loud, even to ourselves. Chaupai's second line asks for exactly that wish to be fulfilled. Today: the heart's wish.
screen: `A CHILD'S LIST OF WISHES.` → `THE LIST GETS SHORTER WITH AGE.` → `THE DEEPEST WISH, UNDERNEATH.`

segments.voice: The line is pooran hoe chit kee ichhaa. Pooran: full, complete, fulfilled. Chit: the mind, the heart, your inner awareness. Ichhaa: wish, longing. May the wish of my heart be fulfilled. This might surprise you. Sikh teaching is often wary of wanting. The Guru Granth Sahib warns again and again about trishna, the thirst that never stops, the craving that eats a life. So how can Chaupai ask God to fulfill a wish? Because of the very next line. In paraphrase: may my mind remain at your feet. The two lines come as a pair. The wish the prayer means isn't the puppy or the bike. It's the deepest one, the wish to stay close to the One. In Sikh imagery, the feet are the place of humility and nearness, where you sit when you've stopped trying to be in charge. And later in the same prayer, the wish comes back in a lovely form. In paraphrase: may my hope be fulfilled, and may my thirst for your praise remain. Think about that. A prayer that asks for one thirst never to be quenched. Every other craving, the tradition says, leaves you emptier. This one is the opposite. It's the only thirst that fills you while it stays a thirst. So the line isn't a blank check. It's a question with an answer folded inside it. What does your heart actually want, underneath the list? Chaupai's answer is to stay at the feet, and to keep wanting that.
screen: `POORAN HOE CHIT KEE ICHHAA.` · `WARY OF THIRST, YET ASKING A WISH.` · `THE PAIR: MY MIND AT YOUR FEET.` · `THE ONE THIRST TO KEEP.` · then, large: `THE HEART'S WISH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your deepest wish. Sit and breathe slowly. Let the surface wishes come up first, the things you want this week, this year. Let them pass, one by one, like cars going by. Then ask a quieter question: underneath all of those, what do I want most? Give it time. It might be to be at peace, to be close to someone, to be close to God, to be good. When something comes that feels true, name it to yourself in a few words. If you pray, you can offer it with Waheguru. If you don't, just hold it. The bell holds the time.
The heart's wish. Pooran hoe chit kee ichhaa: may my heart's longing be fulfilled, paired with the line that names it, to stay at the Lord's feet.
Your line: the heart's wish. Today, when you catch yourself wanting something small, ask what deeper wish is underneath it, and whether you're feeding that one. Day three hundred seventy-two.

373.title: The enemies within and without
373.hook: the prayer asks for enemies to be ended; many read them also as the five thieves inside
373.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite these lines of Chaupai Sahib daily, understanding the enemies both as outward threats and as the five thieves: lust, anger, greed, attachment and ego.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the heart's wish, and your line was the heart's wish itself. Did you find the deeper wish under a small one? Today the prayer turns to something harder. Day three hundred seventy-three.

Anandpur, in the last years of the sixteen hundreds. The town where the Tenth Guru lives sits in the hills, and the hills are full of trouble. Neighboring kings resent him. Imperial armies will later come. There will be sieges, hunger, a night when the town has to be left behind. These aren't metaphors. They're men with weapons, and they're coming. And in this world, the Guru writes a prayer that asks, plainly, for enemies to be ended. It's one of the lines people stumble over when they first read Chaupai. Today: the enemies within and without.
screen: `ANANDPUR, IN THE HILLS.` → `REAL ARMIES, REAL SIEGES.` → `A PRAYER ABOUT ENEMIES.`

segments.voice: The lines come right after the heart's wish. In paraphrase: destroy all my enemies; save me with your own hand. May my family live in peace, and all my servants and Sikhs. A little later: protect me with your own hand, and end all my foes this very day. The word for enemy here is dusht, the wicked, the one who means harm. Sikhs read these lines in two ways, and they don't have to choose. The first reading is the plain one. The Guru and his community faced real violence, and this is the prayer of a leader asking God to protect his people from those who would kill them. Sikhs don't apologize for that. Asking for protection from harm isn't hatred. The second reading goes inside. The Guru Granth Sahib speaks again and again of five thieves living in every person: lust, anger, greed, attachment and ego. They break in at night, the scripture says, and rob the house of its treasure. Many Sikhs, saying Chaupai every day, hear the enemies as those five too. The dusht that does you the most harm on an ordinary Tuesday probably isn't an army. It's your own anger at the driver who cut you off, or the greed that keeps you scrolling, or the ego that can't say sorry. What's notable is where the prayer puts the fight. It doesn't say, let me destroy them. It says, you destroy them, and save me with your hand. The battle, inner or outer, is handed over. The enemy within doesn't go because you hate it. It goes when you're held by something stronger.
screen: `DESTROY MY ENEMIES; SAVE ME.` · `READING ONE: REAL ARMIES.` · `READING TWO: THE FIVE THIEVES.` · `YOU DESTROY THEM; HOLD ME.` · then, large: `END THE ENEMY WITHIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one inner enemy. Sit and breathe slowly. Think of the five thieves: lust, anger, greed, attachment, ego. Don't make a list of all your faults. Just notice which one has been busiest in you lately. Which one robbed you this week? Name it, simply, in one word. Then, instead of fighting it, picture handing it over, the way the prayer does. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you do. If you don't, just let your grip on it loosen a little. The bell holds the time.
The enemies within and without. Chaupai's lines asking for enemies to be ended: real armies for the Guru, and for many Sikhs, the five thieves inside too.
screen: `THE ENEMIES WITHIN AND WITHOUT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: end the enemy within. Today, when the enemy you named shows up, notice it, name it under your breath, and hand it over before it takes anything. Day three hundred seventy-three.

374.title: Keep my Sikhs
374.hook: sevak sikh hamaare taareeh: carry my servants and Sikhs across (Chaupai)
374.tomorrow: The one who spreads and gathers
374.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this line within Chaupai Sahib daily; Sikh prayer, especially the Ardas, typically widens from oneself to family, community and finally the good of all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the enemies within and without, and your line, end the enemy within. Did the one you named show up? Today, the prayer turns outward again, to people. Day three hundred seventy-four.

Picture a wide river in flood, the kind people in Punjab knew well, brown and fast and far too deep to wade. On this bank, everyone you love. On the far bank, safety. There's one boat, and one person who knows how to steer it. You don't ask for yourself first. You ask for them. Take my mother. Take my friend. Take the kids. Get them across. That picture of a river and a crossing runs all through Sikh scripture. And in Chaupai, the Guru uses it to pray for his people. Today: keep my Sikhs.
screen: `A RIVER IN FLOOD.` → `ONE BOAT, ONE PERSON TO STEER.` → `GET THEM ACROSS.`

segments.voice: The line is sevak sikh hamaare taareeahi. Sevak: servants, those who serve. Sikh: learners, disciples. Hamaare: mine. Taareeahi: carry them across. Carry my servants and Sikhs across. The verb is from taarna, to ferry over, to bring someone safely to the other shore. In the Guru Granth Sahib, the world is often pictured as a vast, terrifying ocean, and the Guru, or the Name, as the boat that carries people over it. So when the Tenth Guru prays this line, he's doing something tender. He's a Guru, and he is praying for his disciples, asking God to carry them where he can't carry them himself. Look at how the prayer's circle has been widening. First, protect me. Then, may my family live in peace. Then, all my servants and Sikhs. A few lines on, may my hope be fulfilled, and on it goes. That widening is a very Sikh pattern. The Ardas, the prayer that closes Sikh gatherings, does the same thing. It names the Gurus, the martyrs, the community, and then ends by asking for the good of all, everyone, without exception. You met that on day three hundred thirty. Prayer, in this tradition, almost never stays small. Notice one more thing. This is a prayer said by the community itself, every morning and evening. So when a Sikh recites it, they're saying a prayer the Guru prayed for them. Carry them across. It lands in a different way when you know you're one of the them.
screen: `SEVAK SIKH HAMAARE TAAREEAHI.` · `TAARNA: TO FERRY ACROSS.` · `THE CIRCLE WIDENS: ME, FAMILY, SIKHS.` · `A PRAYER THE GURU PRAYED FOR THEM.` · then, large: `CARRY THEM ACROSS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for a friend by name. Sit and breathe slowly. Bring one friend to mind, someone who's in a hard river right now. Illness, grief, a bad job, a lonely stretch. See their face. Say their name, quietly, out loud if you can. If you pray, you can hold that name in Waheguru, or say the line, carry them across. If you don't pray, simply hold them in your attention for a while and wish them safely to the other bank. Then, if it feels right, let the circle widen: one more name, then everyone in a river like theirs. The bell holds the time.
Keep my Sikhs. Sevak sikh hamaare taareeahi: carry my servants and Sikhs across, the Guru praying for his people over the river.
Your line: carry them across. Today, send that friend a short message, no advice, just letting them know they were held in mind this morning. Day three hundred seventy-four.

375.title: The one who spreads and gathers
375.word: The one who spreads and gathers
375.hook: the Creator spreads creation out and draws it back into Himself (Chaupai)
375.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite these verses of Chaupai Sahib daily, and Sikh teaching describes creation as flowing out from the One and merging back into the One.

segments.voice: Yesterday, keep my Sikhs, and your line, carry them across. Did you send that friend a message? Today Chaupai widens all the way, to the whole of creation. Day three hundred seventy-five.

Watch a jellyfish move. It opens, wide and slow, like an umbrella, and then it closes, pulling itself in, and in that closing it moves forward. Open, close. Spread out, gather in. Or watch your own chest for a few seconds. It's doing the same thing. Out, in. Out, in. Lungs, tides, seasons, a beating heart. A huge amount of the living world runs on that one rhythm. Chaupai takes that rhythm and applies it to the biggest thing there is. Today: the one who spreads and gathers.
screen: `A JELLYFISH OPENS AND CLOSES.` → `OUT, IN. LUNGS, TIDES, A HEART.` → `THE RHYTHM AT THE BIGGEST SCALE.`

segments.voice: In the middle of Chaupai, the prayer stops asking for a moment and simply looks at God. In paraphrase: when the Creator spreads creation out, beings take bodies beyond number. And when, at any time, you draw it back in, all bodies merge back into you. The two old words are udkarakh, spreading out, and aakarakh, drawing in. Out, and in. The whole universe, in this picture, is the Creator's long breath. Breathe out, and there are galaxies, rivers, people, ants. Breathe in, and everything returns to the One it came from. That's a big idea, and it echoes something you met in the Japji. Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that with a single word the Creator made the vast expanse, and from it a million rivers flowed. Creation in Sikh thought isn't a machine built once and left to run. It flows out of the One, and it's held in the One the whole time. Now, why is this in a prayer for protection? Because it changes what being kept means. If everything came out of the One and returns to the One, then nothing that happens to you happens outside God. Even the drawing in, the ending of things, which frightens us most, is described as merging, not vanishing. Bodies merge back into you. That doesn't make loss painless. Sikhs grieve like everyone else. But it puts the loss inside something larger and kinder. The same hand that spread you out is the hand that gathers you in. And the line asks you to see your own breath as a small copy of that.
screen: `THE PRAYER STOPS ASKING AND LOOKS.` · `UDKARAKH: SPREADING OUT.` · `AAKARAKH: DRAWING BACK IN.` · `EVEN THE ENDING IS MERGING.` · then, large: `SPREAD AND GATHERED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe out, then in. Start with the out-breath. Let it go long and slow, all the way, as if you're spreading something out into the room. Pause for a beat. Then let the in-breath come by itself, gathering back. Do that again. Out, spreading. In, gathering. Don't force the rhythm. Let it be the rhythm your body already knows. If you pray, you can let Waheguru ride on the breath, wahe on the way out, guru on the way in. If you don't, just watch the two halves of each breath. The bell holds the time.
The one who spreads and gathers. Udkarakh and aakarakh: the Creator spreads creation out into countless bodies, and draws it all back to merge in the One.
screen: `THE ONE WHO SPREADS AND GATHERS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: spread and gathered. Today, each time you step through a doorway, take one slow breath out and one in, and remember the bigger breath it copies. Day three hundred seventy-five.

376.title: Knower of every heart
376.hook: ghat ghat ke antar kee jaanat: He knows every heart and recognizes the pain of good and bad alike (Chaupai)
376.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this line within Chaupai Sahib morning and evening, and Sikh scripture often names God as antarjami, the inner knower of every heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the one who spreads and gathers, and your line, spread and gathered. Did the doorways remind you? Today, a line about being known, all the way down. Day three hundred seventy-six.

There's a particular loneliness in being misunderstood. You did something for a good reason, and someone took it the worst way. Or you're carrying a pain nobody can see, so people treat you as if you're fine. Or, harder, you did something wrong, and you know it, and nobody can see the mess of reasons and hurt underneath. Most of us walk around partly hidden, even from the people who love us. Sometimes, especially from them. Chaupai has a line for exactly that hiddenness, and it goes further than you'd expect. Today: knower of every heart.
screen: `THE LONELINESS OF BEING MISUNDERSTOOD.` → `PAIN NOBODY CAN SEE.` → `PARTLY HIDDEN, EVEN FROM LOVED ONES.`

segments.voice: The line, transliterated, is ghat ghat ke antar kee jaanat, bhale bure kee peer pachhaanat. Ghat ghat: every vessel, every body, every heart. Ke antar kee jaanat: knows what's inside. Bhale bure: the good and the bad. Kee peer pachhaanat: recognizes the pain of. He knows what's within every heart, and recognizes the pain of the good and the bad alike. The first half is something Sikh scripture says often. God is antarjami, the inner knower, the one who sees from inside. But the second half is the surprise. The pain of the bad. Not just the good person's suffering. The wrongdoer's too. Think about what that means. The person who hurt you has a pain underneath it, and in this line, God recognizes that as well. It doesn't excuse anything. The same prayer has just asked for wrongdoers to be stopped. But it refuses to pretend that anyone, good or bad, is only their actions. Peer, the word for pain here, is close to an ordinary Punjabi word for an ache, the kind you'd mention to a doctor. That's how close this knowing is. And here's the other side of it. If the One knows every heart, then you are known, completely. Your good reasons that nobody saw. Your hidden ache. Even the tangle behind the thing you're ashamed of. For many people that sounds frightening. Chaupai sets it inside a prayer for protection, so it's meant to sound like rest. You don't have to explain yourself here. You're already understood.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be known, and rest. Sit and breathe slowly. Bring to mind something about yourself that nobody fully understands. An old hurt. A reason you've never said out loud. A worry you carry quietly. You don't need to fix it or explain it. Just let it be there, in the open. Then picture it already seen, completely, by someone who isn't shocked. If you pray, you can say Waheguru and let the One who knows every heart hold it. If you don't, just practice not hiding it from yourself. The bell holds the time.

Your line: he knows the pain. Today, when someone acts badly, wonder for one second about the pain underneath, without excusing it. Day three hundred seventy-six.

377.title: Since I held your feet
377.hook: since I grasped Your feet I look to no one else (Chaupai, savaiya)
377.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this savaiya as part of Chaupai Sahib, and it is also included in the evening Rehras; touching the feet of elders and teachers is a common sign of deep respect in Punjabi culture.

segments.voice: Yesterday, knower of every heart, and your line, he knows the pain. Did you wonder, once, about someone's ache underneath? Today Chaupai's verse changes shape, near its end. Day three hundred seventy-seven.

Watch a toddler in a crowded place. A busy market, a big family wedding. As long as they're holding on to a parent's leg, they're fine. They'll peer out at the noise and the strangers, even smile. The second they let go and lose sight of that leg, the whole world becomes terrifying. It's not that the crowd changed. What changed was whether they were holding on. Near the end of Chaupai, the meter shifts into a savaiya, a longer, rolling line, and the poet describes exactly that kind of holding on. Today: since I held your feet.
screen: `A TODDLER HOLDING A PARENT'S LEG.` → `LET GO, AND THE CROWD IS TERRIFYING.` → `WHAT CHANGED WAS THE HOLDING ON.`

segments.voice: In paraphrase, the verse begins: since I grasped your feet, I have not brought anyone else under my eye. Feet again. You met them in the second line of the prayer, where the mind rests at the Lord's feet. Here the poet doesn't just rest there. He has grabbed hold. In South Asian custom, touching or holding someone's feet is what you do before a person you deeply honor: a grandparent, a teacher. To grasp them and not let go is the gesture of someone who has decided where they belong. Then the verse goes on. In paraphrase: many voices, many books and teachings, tell of many views, and I have not taken any one of those views as my own; by your grace, O sword-bearer, I have not said this, it is all your own telling. Two things are worth hearing carefully here. First, this isn't a dismissal of other people's scriptures. The Guru Granth Sahib itself holds the words of Hindu and Muslim saints beside the Gurus. The verse is about where the poet's own eyes rest, not a ruling on anyone else's. When you're holding on to the feet, you stop shopping among opinions. Second, look at the last line: I have not said this; it's all you. The Tenth Guru, poet, leader, founder of the Khalsa, signs the verse by saying it isn't his. That's the posture of someone holding on to feet. And one good word for it is trust. Not a list of things believed. A grip. Since I held your feet, the crowd has stopped being frightening.
screen: `SINCE I GRASPED YOUR FEET.` · `HOLDING FEET: DEEP HONOR.` · `NOT A RULING ON OTHER BOOKS.` · `I HAVE NOT SAID THIS; IT'S ALL YOU.` · then, large: `HELD AT THE FEET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one thing to trust. Sit and breathe slowly. Notice how many things you're half-holding right now: plans, worries, opinions, backup plans for the backup plans. You don't have to drop them all. Just choose one thing to trust today, fully, the way a child holds a leg in a crowd. It might be God, if you pray. It might be a person who has never let you down, or the fact that you've come through hard days before. Hold it in your mind, firmly. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you do. The bell holds the time.
Since I held your feet. Chaupai's savaiya: since I grasped your feet, I look to no one else, and what I've said was never mine.

378.title: Every other door
378.hook: leaving every other door, I have come to Yours; keep my honor (Chaupai, dohra)
378.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this closing dohra as part of Chaupai Sahib and Rehras, and some say it on its own in moments of fear as a short prayer for protection.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the feet, and your line, held at the feet. This week: the heart's wish, the enemy within, carry them across, spread and gathered, he knows the pain, held at the feet. Today, the very last couplet. Day three hundred seventy-eight.

Think of how many doors you've knocked on in your life. Literal ones: the job interviews, the landlord, the new neighbor. And the other kind: the friend you hoped would understand, the qualification you hoped would make you enough, the achievement that was going to fix everything. Some opened. Some didn't. Some opened onto rooms that turned out to be empty. Most people have a long list of doors behind them. Chaupai ends with someone standing at the end of that list, having tried them all, and standing now at one last door. Today: every other door.
screen: `ALL THE DOORS YOU'VE KNOCKED ON.` → `SOME OPENED ONTO EMPTY ROOMS.` → `ONE LAST DOOR.`

segments.voice: The closing couplet, a dohra, goes like this in paraphrase: leaving every other door, I have taken hold of your door. You who have taken my arm, keep my honor. Gobind is your servant. Duaar means door. Sagal duaar, every door. Tuhaaro duaar, your door. And there's that picture from day three hundred seventy-one: baanh gahe, the one who has taken my arm. In Punjabi, to take someone's arm is a promise of protection, the kind you don't walk away from. So the couplet says: you made a promise when you took my arm; keep it, keep my honor. Laaj, the word for honor here, is close to a sense of dignity and good name. It's a very human thing to ask. Don't let me be shamed. And then the signature. Gobind is your servant. This is Guru Gobind Singh, signing the last line of his prayer not as Guru, not as leader of the Khalsa, but as Gobind das, the servant. It's the same humility as yesterday's line, I have not said this. Notice the sequence. The prayer began with a hand. Protect me, giving me your hand. It ends with an arm, taken. The heart's wish was to stay at the feet. It ends at the door, having left every other. A whole prayer, and it's really one movement: a person walking past every other option to the one place they want to be kept. That's why many Sikhs say this couplet on its own, in moments of fear, as the shortest form of the whole Chaupai.
screen: `LEAVING EVERY OTHER DOOR.` · `YOU WHO TOOK MY ARM, KEEP MY HONOR.` · `GOBIND IS YOUR SERVANT.` · `FROM A HAND TO AN ARM, TO A DOOR.` · then, large: `YOUR DOOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand still at a doorway. Get up, if you can, and go stand in an open doorway in your home. Stand right in the frame. Feel the threshold under your feet. Behind you, one room. In front, another. Breathe slowly. Think of the doors you've knocked on, the ones that opened and the ones that didn't. Then let them go, one by one. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, standing at this door. If you don't, just notice how it feels to stop knocking and simply stand. The bell holds the time.
Every other door. Chaupai's last couplet: leaving every other door I have come to yours; you who took my arm, keep my honor. Gobind is your servant.
Your line: your door. Today, each time you pass through a doorway, pause half a second in the frame and remember which door you're standing at. Day three hundred seventy-eight.
